steelman: Smart TV operating systems (Tizen, webOS, Android TV) are known to accumulate corrupted cache, stale CDN tokens, or broken manifest files in streaming apps over time. This internal degradation can produce buffering that appears intermittent or time-correlated if background refresh processes run on fixed schedules. Two prior factory-reset successes on the same device provide genuine inductive evidence that TV-internal state can be the culprit. Moreover, a degraded TV app might fail to buffer gracefully through any moderate congestion that a healthy app would handle — so in a 'coexistence' framing, the TV's internal state could be a contributing co-factor even when another device also stresses the uplink. A senior technician might reasonably say: 'Rule out the known-fixable TV-internal state first before investigating the network.'
mechanism_if_any: TV-internal app/OS state degradation (corrupted cache, stale tokens) causing buffering — a real mechanism, but one that operates entirely within the TV and has no pathway to the separate device's bandwidth consumption that the router identifies as the uplink saturator. The coexistence argument is theoretically possible but does not survive the focal evidence.
notes: The xbase focal feature closes the distractor's pathway decisively: the router traffic monitor attributes uplink saturation specifically to a different device during exactly the symptomatic hours. A factory reset on the TV cannot free bandwidth consumed by a separate device. The only way the distractor direction could survive is if the TV-internal degradation were a co-cause alongside the other device — but the focal evidence assigns the uplink congestion entirely to the other device, leaving TV-internal state as an unsupported dormant hypothesis. The structural break between past cases (no other device implicated; reset fixed it) and the present case (another device identified) is precisely the causal distinction the focal feature exposes. Seed passes this lens. No repair needed.
